name: Allosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877 during the Bone Wars.
• The first nearly complete skeleton was discovered in 1883 by M. P. Felch in Colorado.
• The Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah has yielded thousands of Allosaurus bones since the 1920s.
interestingFacts: Its teeth were serrated and shaped like blades.
The skull had unique ridges or 'horns' above the eyes.
It is the state fossil of Utah.

name: Ceratosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Described by O.C. Marsh in 1884 based on a nearly complete skeleton from Colorado.
• A notable specimen was found in the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry.
• Fossils have been discovered in North America, with possible remains in Portugal and Tanzania.
interestingFacts: It had a prominent horn on its snout.
Ceratosaurus possessed osteoderms along its back.
It likely competed with Allosaurus for prey.

name: Dilophosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered by Sam Welles in 1942 in the Navajo Nation, Arizona.
• Originally assigned to Megalosaurus before receiving its current name in 1970.
• In 2020, a comprehensive study clarified its anatomy, showing it was more robust than previously thought.
interestingFacts: It sported a pair of rounded crests on its skull.
Contrary to popular media, there is no evidence it spat venom.
It was one of the earliest large predatory dinosaurs.

name: Megalosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• The first genus of non-avian dinosaur to be validly named (1824 by William Buckland).
• Early discoveries in Oxfordshire, England, were initially interpreted as giant lizards.
• It became a 'wastebasket taxon' in the 19th and 20th centuries for many unclassified theropods.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'Great Lizard'.
It was one of the original three genera used to define 'Dinosauria'.
True Megalosaurus fossils are only known from the Middle Jurassic of England.

name: Cryolophosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1990-91 during a field expedition in Antarctica led by William Hammer.
• Officially named in 1994, it was the first meat-eating dinosaur found in Antarctica.
• Additional material was recovered during subsequent expeditions in the 2000s.
interestingFacts: Known as 'Elvisaurus' due to its pompadour-like crest.
It lived in a relatively temperate Antarctic climate.
It is the largest known Early Jurassic theropod.

name: Monolophosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1981 by a Canadian-Chinese expedition in Xinjiang, China.
• Described and named in 1993 by Zhao Xijin and Philip J. Currie.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton with an articulated skull.
interestingFacts: It had a single large crest running down the midline of its snout.
The crest was heavily pneumatized (hollow).
It lived in an environment with deep lakes and rivers.

name: Torvosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1972 by Jim Jensen and Kenneth Stadtman in Colorado.
• Described in 1979 by Peter Galton and Jensen.
• A second species, T. gurneyi, was later identified from Portugal.
interestingFacts: It was one of the largest predators of its time.
It had exceptionally powerful jaws and large teeth.
Torvosaurus competed with Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus in the Morrison Formation.

name: Ornitholestes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1900 at the Bone Cabin Quarry in Wyoming.
• Described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1903.
• Only one nearly complete skeleton is known.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'bird robber'.
It was a small, fast, and agile predator.
Contrary to early restorations, it likely did not have a horn on its nose.

name: Compsognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• The first specimen was discovered in the 1850s in the Solnhofen limestone of Germany.
• A larger, second specimen was found in France in 1971.
• It was historically considered the smallest known dinosaur for over a century.
interestingFacts: It was a very small, bipedal carnivore.
Its fossils were found with the remains of small lizards in their stomachs.
It lived on an archipelago in a shallow tropical sea.

name: Guanlong
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2000 in the Junggar Basin, Xinjiang, China.
• Named in 2006 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
• Two specimens, an adult and a juvenile, were found together.
interestingFacts: It is one of the earliest known tyrannosauroids.
It possessed a large, fragile crest on its head.
Its name means 'crowned dragon'.

name: Proceratosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1910 in Gloucestershire, England.
• Initially thought to be an ancestor of Ceratosaurus (hence the name) when described in 1926.
• In 2010, it was reclassified as an early tyrannosauroid.
interestingFacts: It possessed a small crest on its snout.
It is one of the oldest known members of the tyrannosaur lineage.
Only a partial skull has been found.

name: Metriacanthosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 19th century in the Oxford Clay of England.
• Originally classified as a species of Megalosaurus in 1923.
• Alick Walker established the genus Metriacanthosaurus in 1964.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'moderately-spined lizard'.
It had tall neural spines on its back, though not forming a full sail.
It was a medium-sized apex predator of its ecosystem.

name: Yangchuanosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1977 by a construction worker in Sichuan, China.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton with a skull.
• Additional specimens have been found in the Dashanpu Dinosaur Quarry.
interestingFacts: It was a large theropod similar in appearance to Allosaurus.
It had bony ridges and bumps on its snout.
It preyed on large sauropods and stegosaurs.

name: Eustreptospondylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 1871 in a clay pit near Oxford, England.
• It was shuffled between several genera, including Megalosaurus, before Alick Walker named it in 1964.
• It remains one of the most complete theropod skeletons found in Europe.
interestingFacts: It lived in an island environment.
It may have scavenged marine carcasses that washed ashore.
The single known specimen is considered a subadult.

name: Piatnitzkysaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1977 by José Bonaparte in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, Argentina.
• Described in 1979 as an early allosauroid or megalosauroid.
• Two partial skeletons are known.
interestingFacts: It was a medium-sized bipedal predator.
It represents one of the few known Middle Jurassic theropods from South America.
It shares primitive traits with basal tetanurans.

name: Marshosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1976 at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
• Named by James Madsen in 1976 in honor of O.C. Marsh.
• Known from sparse, fragmentary remains.
interestingFacts: It was a medium-sized predator in the Morrison Formation.
It was rarer than competitors like Allosaurus.
Its exact taxonomic position within tetanurans is debated.

name: Stokesosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1974 at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry, Utah.
• Named by James Madsen after geologist William Lee Stokes.
• Primarily known from a pair of distinct ilia (pelvic bones).
interestingFacts: It is an early member of the tyrannosauroid family.
It was a small, agile predator.
Similar fossils found in England were later reclassified as a separate genus, Juratyrant.

name: Tanycolagreus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1995 at the Bone Cabin Quarry West in Wyoming.
• Originally thought to be Coelurus, it was named as a new genus in 2005.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skull and skeleton.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'long-limbed hunter'.
It was slightly larger and more robust than its relative Ornitholestes.
It had a long, low skull compared to other small theropods.

name: Sciurumimus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in a limestone quarry in Bavaria, Germany.
• Described in 2012 by Oliver Rauhut and colleagues.
• The single specimen is an exceptionally preserved juvenile.
interestingFacts: The fossil preserves filamentous feathers, especially along the tail.
Its name means 'squirrel mimic' due to its bushy tail.
Initially thought to be a megalosauroid, it may be a primitive coelurosaur.

name: Juravenator
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1998 in the Solnhofen limestone in Germany.
• Named in 2006 by Ursula Göhlich and Luis Chiappe.
• The specimen is a nearly complete juvenile skeleton.
interestingFacts: Its fossil shows patches of scaly skin, suggesting a lack of feathers in some areas.
It had unusually large eyes, suited for nocturnal hunting.
It was a very small, agile predator.

name: Brachiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1900 in the Grand River Canyon, Colorado by Elmer Riggs.
• Named Brachiosaurus altithorax in 1903.
• Much of its popular image was historically based on African fossils later reassigned to Giraffatitan.
interestingFacts: Its forelimbs were significantly longer than its hindlimbs.
It held its neck vertically to browse on high canopy vegetation.
It had a distinctive nasal arch on its skull.

name: Diplodocus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1877 in Colorado by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Williston.
• Described by O.C. Marsh in 1878.
• The famous 'Dippy' cast is based on a specimen found in 1899 in Wyoming.
interestingFacts: It had an exceptionally long, whip-like tail.
Its center of gravity allowed it to rear up on its hind legs.
Its teeth were peg-like and restricted to the front of the jaw.

name: Apatosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered and named by O.C. Marsh in 1877 in Colorado.
• For over a century, its skeleton was mounted with the wrong skull (that of a Camarasaurus).
• A correct skull was finally mounted on skeletons in the late 1970s.
interestingFacts: It had a very robust, heavily built skeleton compared to Diplodocus.
Its tail may have been able to crack like a whip, producing a loud sound.
It was an abundant herbivore in the Morrison Formation.

name: Brontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Named by O.C. Marsh in 1879 from a specimen found at Como Bluff, Wyoming.
• In 1903, it was synonymized with Apatosaurus and the name fell out of formal use.
• A comprehensive study in 2015 reinstated Brontosaurus as a valid, separate genus.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'thunder lizard'.
It had a slightly thinner and less robust neck than Apatosaurus.
It is one of the most culturally famous dinosaur names.

name: Camarasaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1877 in Colorado by Oramel W. Lucas.
• Named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
• It is the most common sauropod found in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: It had a boxy, blunt skull with large, spoon-shaped teeth.
Its name means 'chambered lizard', referring to hollow chambers in its vertebrae.
It likely fed on tough, fibrous vegetation.

name: Giraffatitan
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania between 1909 and 1912.
• Originally described as a species of Brachiosaurus (B. brancai) in 1914 by Werner Janensch.
• Elevated to its own genus, Giraffatitan, by Gregory S. Paul in 1988.
interestingFacts: It is one of the tallest known dinosaurs.
A famous, nearly complete skeleton is mounted in the natural history museum in Berlin.
It was adapted for high-browsing on conifer trees.

name: Barosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by early bone hunters for O.C. Marsh in South Dakota in 1889.
• Named in 1890, though more complete remains were found later in Utah.
• Remains have also been controversially attributed to it from Tanzania.
interestingFacts: It is closely related to Diplodocus but had a significantly longer neck.
Its neck vertebrae were exceptionally elongated.
A famous mount at the AMNH shows it rearing up to defend against an Allosaurus.

name: Dicraeosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered during the German Tendaguru expeditions in Tanzania (1909–1912).
• Described by Werner Janensch in 1914.
• Multiple specimens have been recovered, making it well-understood.
interestingFacts: It had tall, bifurcated (Y-shaped) neural spines on its neck and back.
It had a relatively short neck for a sauropod.
It was a low-browser in an ecosystem dominated by taller sauropods.

name: Shunosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1977 in the Dashanpu Formation, Sichuan, China.
• Described in 1983 by Dong Zhiming.
• Over 20 mostly complete skeletons have been excavated.
interestingFacts: It possessed a distinctive tail club with two pairs of short spikes.
It was a relatively small, short-necked sauropod.
It is one of the best-known Middle Jurassic sauropods.

name: Mamenchisaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1952 at a highway construction site in Sichuan, China.
• Described in 1954 by renowned paleontologist C.C. Young.
• Many species have been assigned to the genus, though some may belong to other genera.
interestingFacts: It had one of the longest necks of any known animal, making up half its body length.
Its neck vertebrae were reinforced by long, overlapping cervical ribs.
It was a high-browser of the Asian Jurassic forests.

name: Omeisaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1939 in Sichuan, China.
• Named by C.C. Young in 1939 after Mount Omei.
• Massive bonebeds in the Dashanpu Quarry have yielded numerous skeletons.
interestingFacts: It had a long, heavily built neck.
Some species assigned to it may have had a tail club.
It was a common large herbivore in its ecosystem.

name: Vulcanodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1969 on an island in Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe.
• Described by Michael Raath in 1972.
• Originally thought to be a prosauropod due to associated carnivore teeth, later recognized as scavenged.
interestingFacts: It is one of the earliest known true sauropods.
Its forelimbs retained some primitive traits while its hindlimbs were column-like.
It lived in a volcanic landscape.

name: Patagosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 1970s in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, Argentina.
• Described by José Bonaparte in 1979.
• Remains of at least six individuals were found together, suggesting gregarious behavior.
interestingFacts: It was a basal eusauropod with a relatively short neck.
Adults and juveniles were found together, indicating herd living.
It was a dominant herbivore in its South American ecosystem.

name: Cetiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in England and named by Richard Owen in 1841.
• It was the very first sauropod ever discovered and named.
• Originally, Owen believed it was a giant marine crocodile, hence the name 'whale lizard'.
interestingFacts: Its vertebrae lacked the complex hollow air sacs seen in later sauropods.
It was a primitive sauropod weighing roughly 15 tons.
It serves as an important baseline for understanding early sauropod evolution.

name: Spinophorosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in Niger by a Spanish-German expedition.
• Described in 2009 by Remes and colleagues.
• The holotype is one of the most complete basal sauropod skeletons ever found.
interestingFacts: It originally was thought to have a spiked tail club (thagomizer), but the spikes were later re-identified as collarbones.
It is one of the best-preserved early sauropods.
Its anatomy provides a crucial link between basal sauropodomorphs and eusauropods.

name: Haplocanthosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1901 by William H. Utterback in Colorado.
• Named by John Bell Hatcher in 1903.
• Known from a few incomplete specimens in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: It is considered a primitive macronarian sauropod.
It lacked the extreme specialized features of Diplodocus or Camarasaurus.
It was one of the smaller sauropods of the Morrison Formation.

name: Supersaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1972 by Jim Jensen at the Dry Mesa Quarry in Colorado.
• Named in 1985 based on massive, isolated bones.
• More complete remains found in Wyoming in 1996 confirmed its distinct genus status.
interestingFacts: It is among the longest dinosaurs ever discovered.
It was a diplodocid, closely related to Apatosaurus.
Its neck vertebrae were exceptionally elongated and robust.

name: Suuwassea
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 in Montana by a University of Pennsylvania expedition.
• Named in 2004 by J.D. Harris and Peter Dodson.
• The name comes from a Native American word meaning 'ancient thunder'.
interestingFacts: It is a primitive member of the dicraeosaurid family.
It possessed an extra opening (foramen) in its skull of unknown function.
It provides evidence for early diplodocoid radiation in North America.

name: Jobaria
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 by Paul Sereno's expedition in the Sahara Desert, Niger.
• Described in 1999 based on numerous well-preserved skeletons.
• The dating of its formation is debated, ranging from Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.
interestingFacts: It had a relatively short, primitive neck compared to later sauropods.
Its spoon-shaped teeth were adapted for nipping branches.
It was the most common large herbivore in its African environment.

name: Bellusaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Junggar Basin in Xinjiang, China.
• Described in 1987 by Dong Zhiming.
• Seventeen juvenile skeletons were found together in a single quarry.
interestingFacts: The mass grave suggests a herd perished together in a flash flood.
All known specimens are juveniles.
It was a small macronarian sauropod.

name: Stegosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1877 during the Bone Wars by O.C. Marsh.
• The first fossils were found near Morrison, Colorado.
• Complete, articulated skeletons like the 'Sophie' specimen (found in 2003) have greatly refined our understanding of its anatomy.
interestingFacts: It had alternating pentagonal plates along its back.
Its tail featured four prominent spikes (thagomizer) for defense.
It had an unusually small brain cavity relative to its massive body size.

name: Dryosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1876 in Wyoming and sent to O.C. Marsh.
• Described by Marsh in 1894, meaning 'oak lizard' due to leaf-shaped teeth.
• Skeletons of multiple growth stages have been found.
interestingFacts: It was a fast, agile bipedal runner.
It lacked the thumb spikes seen in later iguanodonts.
It was a highly successful, small herbivore of the Morrison Formation.

name: Camptosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1879 by William Harlow Reed in Wyoming.
• Named by O.C. Marsh in 1885.
• It is commonly found in association with Stegosaurus remains.
interestingFacts: It was a heavily built ornithopod that could walk on two or four legs.
It possessed a small, hooved thumb on its hands.
Its beak was toothless, but it had tightly packed cheek teeth.

name: Kentrosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered during the German expeditions to the Tendaguru Formation, Tanzania (1909–1912).
• Described by Edwin Hennig in 1915.
• Hundreds of bones were excavated, allowing for detailed reconstruction.
interestingFacts: Its back was covered in pairs of plates that transitioned into long spikes near the tail.
It featured a prominent spike pointing backward from each shoulder.
It was smaller and more primitively built than Stegosaurus.

name: Heterodontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1961 by a joint South African-British expedition in the Cape Province.
• Named in 1962 by Crompton and Charig.
• Known from nearly complete skulls and skeletons.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'different-toothed lizard'.
It possessed prominent canine-like tusks.
It is one of the most primitive known ornithischians.

name: Scutellosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1971 in the Kayenta Formation, Arizona.
• Described in 1981 by E.H. Colbert.
• Hundreds of small osteoderms (armor plates) were found with the skeleton.
interestingFacts: It is one of the earliest known armored dinosaurs.
It was a small, lightly built, bipedal herbivore.
Its body was covered in parallel rows of small bony scutes.

name: Scelidosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1858 at Charmouth, England, by James Harrison.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1861.
• Exceptionally complete specimens have been recovered from marine deposits.
interestingFacts: It was covered in rows of keeled bony armor.
It is considered an early relative of both ankylosaurs and stegosaurs.
It was a quadrupedal browser with a small head and leaf-shaped teeth.

name: Huayangosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1979 in the Dashanpu Formation, Sichuan, China.
• Described in 1982 by Dong Zhiming and colleagues.
• Multiple specimens, including complete skulls, have been found.
interestingFacts: It is one of the most primitive known stegosaurs.
Unlike later stegosaurs, it retained teeth in the front of its mouth.
It had tall, spike-like plates and large shoulder spikes.

name: Gargoyleosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 in the Bone Cabin Quarry West, Wyoming.
• Named in 1998 by Ken Carpenter and colleagues.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete, well-preserved skull.
interestingFacts: It is one of the earliest and most complete known ankylosaurs.
Its heavily armored skull had prominent horns on the rear corners.
It had a complex network of nasal passages.

name: Othnielosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the late 19th century and heavily revised over time.
• Named in 2007 by Peter Galton to replace the confused taxon Othnielia.
• Known from several partial skeletons in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: It was a small, swift, bipedal herbivore.
It possessed enameled teeth well-adapted to chewing tough vegetation.
Its name honors paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh.

name: Lesothosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Lesotho in the upper Elliot Formation.
• Described by Peter Galton in 1978.
• The holotype includes partial skull and postcranial material.
• Originally thought to be an ornithopod, later recognized as a basal ornithischian.
interestingFacts: One of the earliest known ornithischian dinosaurs.
It had a small, slender body built for fast running.
Its teeth were leaf-shaped, adapted for slicing plant material.

name: Agilisaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lower Shaximiao Formation in Sichuan, China.
• Described by Peng Guangzhou in 1990.
• Holotype is an almost complete, articulated skeleton.
• Named agile lizard due to its lightweight build.
interestingFacts: It had exceptionally long lower leg bones, indicating it was a fast runner.
Features traits of both fabrosaurids and ornithopods.
Possessed a small beak at the front of its mouth.

name: Hexinlusaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Fossils found in the Lower Shaximiao Formation, China.
• Described originally as a species of Yandusaurus in 1983.
• Reclassified and named Hexinlusaurus by Barrett et al. in 2005.
• Name honors Professor He Xinlu.
interestingFacts: A small, basal neornithischian dinosaur.
It had prominent ridges on its teeth for grinding.
Coexisted with larger dinosaurs like Shunosaurus.

name: Chialingosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Upper Shaximiao Formation in Sichuan, China in 1957.
• Described by C.C. Young in 1959.
• One of the first stegosaurs discovered in China.
• The holotype is based on fragmentary remains.
interestingFacts: It was a very slender and primitive stegosaur.
Named after the Jialing River in Sichuan.
Its plates were narrower and more spine-like compared to later stegosaurs.

name: Tuojiangosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Upper Shaximiao Formation of Sichuan, China in 1977.
• Described by Dong Zhiming and colleagues.
• Best-known Asian stegosaur, with a nearly complete skeleton.
• Named after the Tuo River.
interestingFacts: Featured 15 pairs of pointed plates along its back.
Had a distinctive pair of spikes on its shoulders.
Bore a thagomizer with four large spikes at the end of its tail.

name: Dacentrurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in England in 1874.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1875, originally as Omosaurus.
• Renamed Dacentrurus in 1902 by Frederic Lucas.
• Was the very first stegosaur ever discovered.
interestingFacts: Possessed paired spikes rather than plates along most of its back and tail.
Its front limbs were relatively long for a stegosaur.
The pelvis was exceptionally broad to accommodate a large gut.

name: Miragaia
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lourinhã Formation, Portugal.
• Described by Octávio Mateus and colleagues in 2009.
• The holotype consists of the front half of a skeleton, notably the neck.
• Named after the Portuguese parish of Miragaia.
interestingFacts: Had an unusually long neck with at least 17 vertebrae.
Its neck length rivaled some sauropods.
Its back was adorned with paired triangular plates.

name: Hesperosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, USA, in 1985.
• Described by Kenneth Carpenter in 2001.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skull and much of the skeleton.
• Its name means western lizard.
interestingFacts: Closely related to Stegosaurus but had broader, oval-shaped plates.
Its skull was proportionately wider than that of Stegosaurus.
Lived slightly earlier than most Stegosaurus species.

name: Fruitadens
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA, in the 1970s.
• Described by Richard Butler and colleagues in 2010.
• The name means Fruita tooth, after the Fruita Paleontological Area.
• Represented by remains of multiple individuals.
interestingFacts: One of the smallest known ornithischian dinosaurs.
Had canine-like tusks in its lower jaw.
Likely an omnivore, eating both plants and small animals or insects.

name: Nanosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA.
• Described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
• Historically a taxonomic wastebasket taxon.
• Recent studies have clarified its classification among early ornithischians.
interestingFacts: A small, agile, bipedal dinosaur.
Othnielosaurus is often considered a synonym of Nanosaurus.
Used speed to escape from contemporary predators like Allosaurus.

name: Rhamphorhynchus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany.
• First named by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1847.
• Known from numerous perfectly preserved specimens.
• Many specimens preserve soft tissues, including wing membranes.
interestingFacts: Had a long, stiff tail ending in a diamond-shaped vane.
Its jaws were filled with sharp, forward-pointing teeth for catching fish.
Lacked a bony crest on its head.

name: Dimorphodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Dorset, England, in 1828.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1859.
• One of the first pterosaurs ever found.
• Name means two-form tooth, referring to its differentiated teeth.
interestingFacts: Had a remarkably large, deep skull resembling that of a puffin.
Possessed two distinct types of teeth in its jaws.
Its wings were relatively short, suggesting it was not an oceanic soarer.

name: Pterodactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany.
• Described by Cosimo Alessandro Collini in 1784.
• The first pterosaur ever identified as a flying reptile.
• Georges Cuvier later coined the name Ptero-dactyle.
interestingFacts: Had a long, pointed beak filled with small teeth.
It was a short-tailed pterosaur (pterodactyloid).
Likely fed on small fish and invertebrates.

name: Anurognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Ludwig Döderlein in 1923.
• The holotype is a small, nearly complete skeleton on a single slab.
• Its name means without tail and jaw.
interestingFacts: Had a very short skull and broad, frog-like mouth.
Unlike its relatives, it had a very short tail.
Likely an aerial insectivore, similar to modern nightjars.

name: Campylognathoides
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Posidonia Shale of Germany.
• First described in 1894 as a species of Campylognathus.
• Renamed Campylognathoides by Strand in 1928 due to name preoccupation.
• Known from exceptionally preserved skeletons.
interestingFacts: Had an unusually short snout and large eyes.
Its wings were exceptionally long compared to its body.
May have hunted on land or in forests rather than over water.

name: Dorygnathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Posidonia Shale of Germany in the 19th century.
• Described by Johann Andreas Wagner in 1860.
• Its name means spear jaw.
• Known from dozens of well-preserved specimens.
interestingFacts: Had dramatic, exceptionally long, interlocking front teeth.
Its hind limbs were relatively long, suggesting terrestrial capability.
Likely snatched fish from the water surface.

name: Scaphognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• First described by August Goldfuss in 1831.
• Originally assigned to Pterodactylus before getting its own genus.
• Only a few specimens have ever been found.
interestingFacts: Had a broader, more robust skull than its relative Rhamphorhynchus.
Its teeth were vertically oriented rather than pointing forward.
Its brain was relatively large compared to other early pterosaurs.

name: Sordes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Karabastau Formation of Kazakhstan in 1971.
• Described by Aleksandr Grigorevich Sharov.
• The holotype prominently preserved impressions of hair-like structures (pycnofibers).
• The name Sordes pilosus means hairy devil.
interestingFacts: Provided the first undeniable proof that pterosaurs were covered in fluff.
Had a thick coat of pycnofibers over its body and part of its wings.
Was a small, long-tailed pterosaur.

name: Darwinopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2009.
• Named in honor of Charles Darwin on the 200th anniversary of his birth.
• Represented by numerous complete skeletons, including one with an egg.
interestingFacts: A crucial missing link showing modular evolution in pterosaurs.
Had a long tail like early pterosaurs, but the skull of advanced ones.
Exhibited clear sexual dimorphism, with males having head crests.

name: Wukongopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2009.
• Named after Sun Wukong, the Monkey King from Chinese mythology.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton.
interestingFacts: Part of the transitional group connecting basal and advanced pterosaurs.
Had a robust tail and elongated cervical vertebrae.
Likely arboreal, navigating through dense forest environments.

name: Kunpengopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of China.
• Described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2010.
• Named after the Kunpeng, a mythical Chinese creature that transforms from fish to bird.
• Known from well-preserved specimens including an egg.
interestingFacts: Recently discovered to possess an opposable thumb.
The opposable thumb suggests it lived and climbed in trees.
It lacked a bony crest on its head.

name: Ctenochasma
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1852.
• Its name means comb jaw.
• Found primarily in late Jurassic marine deposits.
interestingFacts: Had hundreds of long, thin teeth forming a comb-like structure.
Used its unique jaws to filter-feed on small aquatic organisms.
Was a fully flying equivalent to modern flamingos.

name: Gnathosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Hermann von Meyer in 1833.
• Was originally mistaken for a teleosaurid (marine crocodile).
• Reidentified as a pterosaur by Albert Oppel in 1862.
interestingFacts: Its jaws broadened at the tip into a spoon-like shape.
Possessed over 130 needle-like teeth.
Fed by sweeping its jaws through mud to catch small invertebrates.

name: Cycnorhamphus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone in Germany.
• First named in 1855, but later lumped with Pterodactylus.
• Reinstated as a distinct genus in the mid-20th century.
• Name means swan beak.
interestingFacts: Had unusual jaws with a distinctive upward curve or kink.
Likely used its specialized jaws to crush hard-shelled prey.
Lacked teeth in the front portion of its mouth.

name: Germanodactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Originally assigned to Pterodactylus in 1901.
• Reclassified as its own genus by C.C. Young in 1964.
• Name means German finger.
interestingFacts: Had a prominent bony crest running along the top of its skull.
Its jaws were mostly toothless at the very front.
Likely hunted fish, similar to modern terns.

name: Pterorhynchus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Stephen Czerkas and Ji Qiang in 2002.
• Only one well-preserved specimen has been found.
• The name means wing snout.
interestingFacts: Preserved an intricate, sail-like crest made of keratin.
Had long hair-like pycnofibers with distinct tufts.
Its tail vane was reinforced by elongated scales.

name: Harpactognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, USA.
• Described by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues in 2003.
• Known only from a partial snout.
• Name means snatching jaw.
interestingFacts: One of the few large pterosaurs known from the Morrison Formation.
Had a significant bony crest extending to the tip of its snout.
Its wingspan is estimated to have been around 2.5 meters.

name: Mesadactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA.
• Described by James Jensen and Kevin Padian in 1989.
• Known from fragmentary remains, primarily a synsacrum.
• Name means Mesa finger, after the discovery site at Dry Mesa Quarry.
interestingFacts: One of the earliest recognized pterodactyloid pterosaurs in North America.
Was quite small, with an estimated wingspan under 1 meter.
Its isolated bones were initially confused with bird remains.

name: Jianchangnathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Xin Cheng and colleagues in 2012.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton.
• Closely related to the genus Scaphognathus.
interestingFacts: Had a highly robust lower jaw with a prominent chin.
Only three teeth were present in each maxilla.
Its tail was relatively straight and rigid.

name: Fenghuangopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
• Described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2010.
• Represented by a single, beautifully preserved skeleton.
• Named after the Fenghuang, a mythological Chinese bird.
interestingFacts: A member of the scaphognathine group of pterosaurs.
Had a blunt, short skull packed with vertically oriented teeth.
Provides key insights into early pterosaur diversity in Asia.

name: Liopleurodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England or France.
• Described by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.
• Name means smooth-sided tooth, referring to its tooth enamel.
• Gained fame through its exaggerated depiction in Walking with Dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: A formidable apex predator of the Jurassic seas.
Though famously portrayed as 25 meters long, it actually reached about 6-7 meters.
Had an exceptionally powerful bite force.

name: Plesiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in 1823.
• Described by William Conybeare in 1824.
• The first complete plesiosaur skeleton ever found.
• Its name means near lizard.
interestingFacts: Characterized by a small head, long neck, and four large flippers.
Moved through the water by flying with its flippers, like modern sea turtles.
Its diet consisted mainly of fish and small cephalopods.

name: Ichthyosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in the early 19th century.
• Described by Charles König in 1818.
• The first fully recognized genus of the ichthyosaur group.
• Its name translates to fish lizard.
interestingFacts: Convergent evolution gave it a body shape strikingly similar to a modern dolphin.
Gave birth to live young at sea, as proven by fossilized mothers with embryos.
Had massive eyes reinforced by bony rings for deep-water vision.

name: Ophthalmosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• Hundreds of specimens have been discovered worldwide.
• The name means eye lizard.
interestingFacts: Had the largest eyes relative to body size of any known vertebrate.
Its enormous eyes suggest it hunted in deep, dark waters.
Possessed a teardrop-shaped body built for high-speed swimming.

name: Cryptoclidus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1892.
• Name means hidden collarbone, referring to its small clavicles.
• Known from numerous excellent skeletons.
interestingFacts: Had a surprisingly fragile skull for a marine predator.
Its jaws were lined with dozens of interlocking, needle-like teeth.
Likely fed by trapping small fish and soft-bodied squid.

name: Rhomaleosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Alum Shale Formation of Yorkshire, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• The most famous specimen is named the Barrow Kipper.
• Name means strong lizard.
interestingFacts: A large, robust pliosaur with a powerful build.
Had an internal nasal passage that allowed it to smell underwater.
Hunted other large marine reptiles as well as big fish.

name: Macroplata
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Blue Lias Formation in Warwickshire, England.
• Described by William Elgin Swinton in 1930.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skeleton.
• Its name means big plate, referring to its large shoulder bones.
interestingFacts: Had an unusually long neck for an early pliosaur.
Its skull was robust and crocodilian in shape.
Reached about 4.5 meters in length.

name: Peloneustes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The name translates roughly to mud swimmer.
• Known from numerous specimens.
interestingFacts: A relatively small pliosaur, measuring around 3 meters long.
Had fewer, more robust teeth than its relatives.
Specialized in hunting hard-shelled prey like ammonites and belemnites.

name: Pliosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1841.
• It is the type genus for the entire group of short-necked plesiosaurs.
• The famous Predator X was eventually classified as a species of Pliosaurus.
interestingFacts: An enormous apex predator of the Late Jurassic.
Its skull could reach over 2 meters in length.
Its bite force was powerful enough to crush a car.

name: Simolestes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England in the 19th century.
• Described by Charles William Andrews in 1909.
• Name means snub-nosed thief.
• A very complete skeleton was found in a brick pit in Peterborough.
interestingFacts: Had a remarkably short, blunt snout.
Its jaw muscles were exceptionally large, giving it a very powerful bite.
Likely specialized in twisting chunks of flesh off large prey.

name: Temnodontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The first ichthyosaur skull ever found belonged to this genus.
• Name means cutting-tooth lizard.
interestingFacts: One of the largest known ichthyosaurs, reaching up to 12 meters.
An apex predator that fed on other marine reptiles and large cephalopods.
Possessed large, robust teeth with distinct cutting edges.

name: Stenopterygius
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Posidonia Shale of Holzmaden, Germany.
• Described by Otto Jaekel in 1904.
• Known from hundreds of beautifully preserved skeletons.
• Many specimens perfectly preserve body outlines and soft tissues.
interestingFacts: Soft tissue preservation proved ichthyosaurs had a shark-like dorsal fin.
Multiple specimens died while in the act of giving birth.
Was highly streamlined for rapid, sustained swimming.

name: Eurhinosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Posidonia Shale of Germany.
• Described by O. Abel in 1909.
• A well-known relative to the similar Excalibosaurus.
• Name means well-nosed lizard.
interestingFacts: Its upper jaw was twice as long as its lower jaw, resembling a swordfish.
Its teeth pointed outward, forming a dangerous, saw-like edge.
Likely used its upper jaw to slash through schools of fish.

name: Excalibosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lower Lias of Somerset, England, in 1984.
• Described by Christopher McGowan in 1986.
• Named after Excalibur, King Arthur legendary sword.
• Known from a nearly complete skeleton.
interestingFacts: Like Eurhinosaurus, it had an extremely elongated upper jaw.
Its front flippers were much shorter than those of its relatives.
Helps document the evolutionary transition of swordfish-like ichthyosaurs.

name: Morganucodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in limestone fissures in Glamorgan, Wales, in 1941.
• Described by Walter Kühne in 1949.
• Its name means Glamorgan tooth.
• Thousands of isolated teeth and bones have since been found.
interestingFacts: One of the earliest and most transitional forms between cynodonts and true mammals.
Had a double jaw joint, a hallmark of early mammalian evolution.
Was a tiny, shrew-like animal that hunted insects at night.

name: Castorocauda
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China, in 2004.
• Described by Qiang Ji and colleagues in 2006.
• Preserved remarkably detailed impressions of hair and soft tissue.
• Name means beaver tail.
interestingFacts: The earliest known mammal-like animal with a beaver-like tail and webbed feet.
Provides evidence that early mammaliaforms were highly specialized, not just generalized shrews.
Preserves the oldest known evidence of mammalian hair.

name: Volaticotherium
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Jin Meng and colleagues in 2006.
• The fossil excellently preserved a large gliding membrane.
• Name means ancient gliding beast.
interestingFacts: The earliest known gliding mammal-like animal.
Pushed back the origin of mammalian gliding flight by 70 million years.
Had sharp teeth adapted for a purely insectivorous diet.

name: Fruitafossor
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA, in 2005.
• Described by Zhe-Xi Luo and John Wible.
• Named after the town of Fruita, Colorado, and fossor meaning digger.
• Nicknamed Popeye due to its massive arm bones.
interestingFacts: Had remarkably strong forelimbs adapted for digging, like a modern mole or aardvark.
Its tube-like, rootless teeth were perfectly suited for eating colonial insects like termites.
Shows that early mammals were highly ecologically diverse.

name: Juramaia
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
• Described by Zhe-Xi Luo and colleagues in 2011.
• The fossil preserves a nearly complete skull and skeleton with soft tissue traces.
• Name means Jurassic mother from China.
interestingFacts: The earliest known eutherian (placental) mammal.
Pushed back the divergence date of placental and marsupial mammals by 35 million years.
Its forelimbs indicate it was an agile tree climber.

name: Agilodocodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation in Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Qing-Jin Meng and colleagues in 2015.
• Represented by an incredibly well-preserved skeleton.
• Name means agile docodont.
interestingFacts: An early mammaliaform that was highly adapted for living in trees.
Its teeth suggest it had a specialized diet of tree sap.
Possessed highly flexible wrists and elbows for grasping branches.

name: Barapasaurus
dietDetails: High browser feeding on conifers, cycads, and ferns.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1958 near Pochampally in the Pranhita-Godavari Valley, Telangana, by geologists of the Indian Statistical Institute.
• Over 300 bone specimens representing at least six individual skeletons were excavated between 1960 and 1961.
• Formally described and named in 1975 by Sohan Lal Jain, T. S. Kutty, T. Roy-Chowdhury, and S. Chatterjee.
• The specific epithet honors Rabindranath Tagore, the Nobel laureate poet, on his birth centenary.
interestingFacts: One of the earliest known true sauropods, representing a transitional form between early prosauropods and later giants.
Possessed spoon-shaped teeth with coarse serrations, adapted for stripping tough volcanic vegetation.
A composite skeleton of the species is mounted and displayed at the Geology Museum of the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata.
sizeNotes: Large basal sauropod reaching 12 to 14 meters in length and weighing around 7 metric tonnes.

name: Kotasaurus
dietDetails: Low to medium browser feeding on Jurassic vegetation.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the late 1970s near the village of Yamanpalli in the Mancherial District of Telangana, India.
• Excavations conducted by the Geological Survey of India (GSI) between 1974 and 1982 recovered approximately 840 bone fragments.
• Formally described and named in 1988 by GSI paleontologist P. Yadagiri.
• The skeletal remains represent at least 12 individual dinosaurs found in a communal bonebed.
interestingFacts: Retained some primitive, prosauropod-like features, such as relatively short forelimbs and a less specialized pelvic structure.
Recent 2024 analysis suggested it possessed bony tail clubs, indicating active tail defense mechanisms in early sauropods.
Its reconstructed skeleton is mounted and displayed at the B. M. Birla Science Museum in Hyderabad.
sizeNotes: Estimated length of 14 meters and standing over 5 meters tall.
